headings.title: Introduction to the Vascular System
headings.content: The human body relies on a vast, closed network of plumbing to transport blood everywhere it is needed. This vascular system consists of arteries, capillaries, and veins working together to maintain tissue perfusion, deliver oxygen and nutrients, and remove metabolic waste products. Blood leaves the heart under high pressure, travels through branching conduits to reach the microscopic beds where chemical exchange occurs, and then returns through a low-pressure collection system back to the heart. Without this continuous circulation, cellular hypoxia and necrosis follow rapidly.

headings.title: Arteries and Arterioles
headings.content:
Arteries carry blood away from the heart, typically bearing oxygen-rich blood except in the pulmonary circuit. Because they face the powerful surges of ventricular contraction, their walls are thick, muscular, and highly elastic. 

- **Elastic arteries**: Large vessels near the heart like the aorta that absorb pressure peaks.
- **Muscular arteries**: Medium-sized vessels that distribute blood to specific organs.
- **Arterioles**: Tiny terminal branches that regulate blood flow into capillary beds through vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

headings.title: Capillaries
headings.content:
Capillaries are the microscopic sites of exchange between the blood and surrounding interstitial fluid. Their walls consist of a single layer of endothelial cells resting on a basement membrane, which minimizes diffusion distance for gases, nutrients, and wastes.

- **Continuous capillaries**: Uninterrupted lining found in muscle and skin.
- **Fenestrated capillaries**: Have pores for rapid fluid exchange in kidneys and intestines.
- **Sinusoids**: Leaky, wide vessels found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.

headings.title: Veins and Venules
headings.content:
Veins return blood back toward the heart under low pressure. Because the driving force from the heartbeat has largely faded, veins rely on accessory mechanisms to push blood upward against gravity, especially from the lower extremities.

- **Venules**: Small vessels that collect blood from capillary networks.
- **Medium veins**: Contain one-way valves formed by folds of the endothelium.
- **Skeletal muscle pump**: Contraction of surrounding muscles squeezes veins to propel blood upward.
- **Respiratory pump**: Inhalation creates negative thoracic pressure that draws blood toward the heart.

headings.title: Histology and Structure of Blood Vessel Walls
headings.content:
Most blood vessels share a common three-layered structural plan, known as tunics, though the thickness of each layer varies depending on vessel type and function.

| Tunic Layer | Main Tissue Composition | Primary Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tunica Intima** | Endothelium and connective tissue | Provides a smooth, slick surface to reduce friction |
| **Tunica Media** | Smooth muscle and elastic fibers | Controls vasoconstriction and blood pressure |
| **Tunica Externa** | Collagen and loose connective tissue | Protects and anchors the vessel to surrounding tissue |

headings.title: Hemodynamics and Blood Flow Regulation
headings.content: Hemodynamics describes the physical principles governing blood flow through the body. Flow is directly proportional to the pressure gradient and inversely proportional to vascular resistance. If blood vessels constrict, resistance rises and blood pressure increases. Local tissues also autoregulate their own blood supply based on metabolic needs, releasing chemical signals when oxygen runs low to open up local arterioles.

headings.title: Common Vascular Disorders in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Vascular pathology frequently complicates clinical care. Atherosclerosis involves plaque buildup inside arterial walls, narrowing the lumen and predisposing patients to ischemia, stroke, and myocardial infarction. Chronic venous insufficiency occurs when venous valves fail, leading to pooling, edema, and lower leg ulcerations. Hypertension places chronic mechanical stress on vessel walls, accelerating arterial damage throughout the body.
